lesson.title: Trading Partners: How Double Replacement Reactions Work
lesson.summary: In a double replacement reaction, the positive and negative ions of two ionic compounds swap partners, producing two new compounds while nothing is oxidized or reduced.
lesson.body:
You already know from the Reaction Types Overview that chemists sort reactions into a handful of recognizable families. Double replacement is one of the most common patterns in aqueous chemistry, and it has a distinctive shape: two compounds come together, and their ions trade places. If compound AB reacts with compound CD, the products are AD and CB. Nothing is created or destroyed at the level of atoms, the cations and anions are simply reshuffled into new pairings.

Why does this happen? Ionic compounds are held together by the attraction between oppositely charged ions. When you dissolve two ionic compounds in water, all four types of ions (two cations, two anions) become free to move around independently, since water surrounds and separates them. At that point, an anion has no memory of which cation it originally arrived with. If a new pairing of cation and anion is more stable in that environment, for example because it is insoluble and drops out of solution, or because it forms a gas or a stable molecule like water, that new pairing will form. If neither new pairing offers any advantage over the original, the ions simply stay mixed in solution and no observable reaction occurs. Later chapters will give you tools, the solubility rules, for predicting which case you are in.

To identify the products of a double replacement reaction, first identify the cation and anion in each starting compound, then swap the anions. Consider silver nitrate reacting with sodium chloride: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq). The cations are Ag+ and Na+, the anions are NO3- and Cl-. Swapping partners gives AgCl (silver paired with chloride) and NaNO3 (sodium paired with nitrate). Checking the equation atom by atom: 1 silver on each side, 1 sodium on each side, 1 chlorine on each side, and 1 nitrogen with 3 oxygens on each side. The equation is already balanced with all coefficients equal to 1. In this case, solid silver chloride separates out of solution, a visible sign that a real chemical change has occurred.

Acid base neutralization is another familiar example of double replacement: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). Here the cation like species are H+ and Na+ and the anion like species are Cl- and OH-. Swapping gives NaCl and HOH, which is simply written as water, H2O. Every atom balances on the first try: 1 hydrogen from HCl plus 1 from NaOH equals the 2 hydrogens in H2O, 1 chlorine on each side, 1 sodium on each side, 1 oxygen on each side. Recognizing that neutralization is a double replacement reaction under the hood will make the ionic equations you write in a few chapters feel much less mysterious.
